extra.message: SQL injection via ip and col parameters in Analytics.hits_by_ip raw query — Full database compromise — an attacker can extract all PII (SSN, DoB, bank account numbers), modify records, or drop tables via the admin analytics search form. [verified: hits_by_ip() (analytics.py:54-59) concatenates user-supplied 'ip' and 'col' into a raw SQL string with no sanitization. The admin_analytics view (admin/views.py:71-98) extracts these from request.GET with zero validation and passes them directly. Accessible to any authenticated user via /admin/<id>/analytics/; no compensating control exists.]

Command Injection via filename in Benefits.make_backup os.system call — Remote code execution on the server with the web process's privileges. [verified: Same command-injection sink as the other OS findings; the os.system call at line 56 receives full_file_name and bak_file_path both derived from the attacker's uploaded filename, with zero escaping or validation in the chain from request.FILES to shell execution.]

OS Command Injection via Uploaded Filename — Remote code execution on the server — an attacker uploading a file with a name like `; rm -rf / #.pdf` can execute arbitrary shell commands with the web server's privileges, leading to full system compromise. [verified: uploaded_file.name from request.FILES['myfile'] flows unsanitized into os.system("cp %s %s" % (full_file_name, bak_file_path)) on line 71; only @user_is_authenticated gates the POST /upload/ endpoint — an attacker can self-register, obtain a valid auth_token, and inject shell metacharacters in the filename for direct RCE.]

Missing Authorization: Admin views accessible to any authenticated user — Any authenticated user (including non-admin employees) can access admin dashboard, view all users' data, delete users, modify any user's attributes including is_admin flag, and escalate their own privileges to admin [verified: Same missing admin gate: @user_is_authenticated checks only auth_token→User mapping (app/decorators.py), never user.is_admin, across all admin views.]

Remote Code Execution via eval() on user-supplied class parameter in mobile API — Full remote code execution on the server; attacker can read/write files, exfiltrate the database, or pivot into the network. [verified: Same unfiltered eval(classname) pattern in api_id at views.py line 24: classname from request.GET.get('class') reaches eval() with zero controls — reachable via GET /api/v1/mobile/<id>?class=... .]

Weak Predictable Password Reset Token using MD5 of email address — Attacker can compute valid password reset tokens for any user whose email is known, reset their password, and take over any account [verified: Token at line 33 is `str(user_id) + '-' + MD5(email).hexdigest()` — deterministic, unsalted, no expiry, no invalidation; an attacker who knows a victim's email can compute the token offline and reset the password, achieving account takeover.]

Predictable password reset token via MD5 of email with no expiration or invalidation — Attacker who knows target's email can compute reset token and take over account. [verified: Token at line 37 is `user_id + '-' + MD5(email).hexdigest()` — deterministic, unsalted, never expires, never invalidated; an attacker who knows the email computes the exact token and takes over the account.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads on attacker-controlled User object in password reset — Attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary remote code execution on the server [verified: Same pickle.loads RCE as finding [0]; base64.b64decode(request.POST['user']) at line 73 is fed to pickle.loads with no sanitization, and CSRF does not stop a direct attacker who can first GET a valid token before POSTing the exploit.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file read via unsanitized 'name' parameter in download view — Arbitrary file read on the server; exposure of source code, database file, /etc/passwd, settings.py with secrets. [verified: Same path-traversal sink as finding 0: BASE_DIR + '/' + unsanitized GET['name'] opened via file(); no directory traversal protection or path confinement exists.]

IDOR — Cross-User Profile Update via user_view POST Handler — Full account takeover — any authenticated user can change another user's password, email, and name, then log in as that victim. This grants access to the victim's PII (SSN, DoB, income), payroll data, messages, and admin privileges if the victim is an admin. [verified: The @user_is_authenticated decorator (app/decorators.py:5-14) only verifies a valid auth_token exists but never checks that the authenticated user owns the user_id_form POST field or user_id URL parameter; validate_update_form (app/models/User/user.py:173) also has no ownership validation, so any authenticated user can update another user's password, email, and name via POST to /users/<victim_id>.]

SQL Injection in user_view via raw query with user_id parameter — Attacker can execute arbitrary SQL queries, extract all user data including password hashes, SSNs, bank account numbers, or modify/drop database tables [verified: Identical SQL injection entry point: attacker-controlled POST body user_id_form (line 71) is concatenated via string formatting into the raw SQL executed at lines 75-77. No middleware, decorator, or validation intercepts or sanitizes this input before it reaches the raw query sink.]

DEBUG=True and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] in production configuration — Sensitive information disclosure (SECRET_KEY, database queries, source paths) via debug error pages; Host-header poisoning [verified: DEBUG=True (line 24–25) and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] (line 26–27) are genuine configuration weaknesses on a reachable path; the threat model exempts neither.]

DEBUG=True and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] — Critical Production Misconfiguration — Information disclosure via verbose error pages exposes SECRET_KEY, database structure, file paths, and internal logic to attackers. Combined with wildcard host header, this enables cache poisoning, password reset poisoning, and SSRF via Host header manipulation. [verified: DEBUG=True (line 25) dumps stack traces/local vars/settings to any visitor on error; ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] (line 27) disables Host validation enabling host-header poisoning. Neither is exempted by the threat model.]

DEBUG=True in production settings exposes sensitive debug information — Information disclosure of source code paths, database queries, configuration secrets via error pages; aids further exploitation. [verified: DEBUG=True at line 25 exposes detailed error pages with stack traces, local variables, and settings to any unauthenticated visitor who triggers an exception.]

DEBUG=True and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] in production configuration — Information disclosure via debug error pages; host header injection attacks possible. [verified: DEBUG=True (line 26) and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] (line 28) are both active; debug error pages leak secrets and the wildcard host permits host-header attacks.]

Path Traversal in File Upload Allows Arbitrary File Write — An attacker can upload a file with a crafted filename containing path traversal sequences to write arbitrary content to any location on the filesystem writable by the Django process, potentially achieving remote code execution. [verified: os.path.join(data_path, uploaded_file.name) at line 28 passes the attacker-controlled multipart filename with no sanitization to default_storage.save; Django 1.11 FileSystemStorage does not validate against '../' sequences, allowing arbitrary file writes outside MEDIA_ROOT/data/.]

MD5 used for password hashing instead of a strong adaptive algorithm — Stored password hashes can be cracked in minutes using commodity hardware. If the database is breached (e.g., via SQL injection or path traversal to db.sqlite3), all user passwords are trivially recoverable. [verified: User.authenticate() at line 107 uses unsalted MD5 for password comparison; hash_password() at line 132 also uses unsalted MD5. No salt, no adaptive hashing — database breach yields all passwords near-instantly.]

Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 — Compromised password hashes can be cracked near-instantly using rainbow tables; password reuse across accounts. [verified: Unsalated MD5 password hashing at line 107 in authenticate(); identical passwords produce identical hashes, and MD5 is trivially cracked with rainbow tables.]

Unsalted MD5 hashing for passwords, auth tokens, and password-reset tokens — Passwords crackable via rainbow tables; password-reset tokens predictable if email is known; auth tokens forgeable [verified: Unsalted MD5 used for password verification (line 107), auth token generation (line 141 via MD5(email+random)), and password-reset tokens (password_resets/views.py line 45 using MD5(email)). No salt, no adaptive hash; rainbow-table and brute-force attacks are trivial.]

MD5 Password Hashing — Weak Cryptographic Storage — In the event of a database breach, all user passwords can be cracked quickly using commodity hardware and rainbow tables, enabling account takeover across the entire user base and credential-stuffing attacks on other services. [verified: User.authenticate() at line 107 verifies passwords via unsalted hashlib.md5(input_password.encode()).hexdigest(); hash_password() at line 132 also uses unsalted MD5. No salt, no key-stretching, and MD5 is trivially reversible via rainbow tables.]

MD5 Used for Password Hashing and Authentication Token Generation — Password hashes can be efficiently cracked using rainbow tables or GPU-based attacks due to MD5's weaknesses and the lack of salt. Auth tokens can potentially be predicted or collided. [verified: hash_password() at line 132 and authenticate() at line 107 both use unsalted MD5; generate_token() at line 141 uses MD5(email+PRNG). MD5 is broken for collision resistance and fast to brute-force.]

Auth tokens generated with non-cryptographic PRNG (random.randint) — Predictable session tokens enable session hijacking; attacker can compute valid tokens for target accounts. [verified: generate_token() at line 141 uses random.randint(1,1000000) from Python's non-cryptographic random module (Mersenne Twister) to seed MD5 auth tokens; an attacker observing a few tokens can predict future tokens due to the tiny 1M seed space and predictable PRNG state.]

SSN stored and displayed in plaintext, encryption method exists but is never invoked — Full SSN exposure to anyone with database access or via IDOR on the work_info view; regulatory non-compliance. [verified: WorkInfo.SSN is a plaintext CharField; encrypt_ssn() exists but has no signal, no save() override, and is never called by any view or form — the encryption method is dead code. The template renders {{ work_info.SSN }} directly (client-side JS masking is cosmetic, value remains in HTML source), exposing full SSNs in cleartext to anyone with DB or IDOR access.]

Mass Assignment — Privilege Escalation via is_admin Field — Any authenticated user can escalate their own privileges to administrator by including is_admin=True in the POST data, then perform all administrative actions including accessing all users' PII and modifying the entire application database. [verified: admin_update_user passes request.POST.dict() — with only password/password_confirmation popped — directly to User.objects.filter().update(**data) at line 58-62; template/admin/modal.html includes <select name="is_admin"> confirming the field is submitted.]

Missing Authentication on Mobile API endpoint with eval() — Any unauthenticated attacker can send a GET request to /api/v1/mobile/?class=... and achieve remote code execution via eval() without any credentials [verified: Neither api_index nor api_id has @user_is_authenticated or any token check; compare with every other user/admin view and /api/v1/users/ which all enforce auth — the mobile API is fully unauthenticated, exposing serialized model data without credentials.]

Sensitive data exposure — password hashes returned in admin API response — An attacker who obtains a valid admin API token (the token validation is already known to be broken) receives every user's MD5 password hash, enabling offline cracking and credential reuse against other services. [verified: When check_if_valid_token passes (see finding 0), api_index serializes User objects via Django's serializers.serialize("json", ...), which includes every model field — password (MD5 hash) and auth_token — with zero field filtering or redaction. The admin path exposes all users' hashes; the non-admin path exposes the targeted user's hash. No control strips these fields before the HttpResponse.]

Broken API token validation — regex bypass allows token forgery across users — API authentication bypass — attacker can access /api/v1/users/ endpoints as any user [verified: The regex (.*?)-(.*) lacks the DOTALL flag, so . does not match newlines. An attacker with a valid token for user X sends Authorization: Token=Y%0aX-<hash_of_X>; re.search skips Y\n and validates the hash for X, but extrapolate_user splits on - capturing the Y\nX prefix and extracts Y via re.split('[^0-9.]'). No sanitization, middleware, or decorator intervenes — the API endpoints have only @requi]

Broken API token validation regex allows horizontal privilege escalation — API authentication bypass; attacker can access any user's data or, if targeting an admin token hash, retrieve all users' data including passwords. [verified: Same root cause as finding 0: the (.*?)-(.*) regex without DOTALL and the divergence between check_if_valid_token's regex.search and extrapolate_user's split('-')[0] + re.split('[^0-9.]') enable the newline-injection bypass. An attacker holding any valid token escalates horizontally to any user_id with no compensating access control on the API views.]

Missing rate limiting on login, signup, and password reset endpoints — Brute-force password guessing; account lockout bypass; email spam via password reset flooding. [verified: Duplicate of [1]/[4]: no rate limiting anywhere on login (line 22 sessions_index), signup, or forgot_password — confirmed absent across entire project.]

Missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags on auth_token session cookie — Session hijacking via network sniffing, XSS-based cookie theft, or CSRF-based session riding. [verified: Same missing-cookie-flags as [2]/[5]/[8]/[10]/[13]: set_cookie at line 45 omits secure/httponly/samesite flags with no settings.py security overrides.]

Missing Secure and HttpOnly flags on auth_token session cookie — auth_token can be stolen via XSS attacks (missing HttpOnly) or intercepted over unencrypted connections (missing Secure), enabling complete session hijacking [verified: Same missing-cookie-flags finding as [2]/[5]/[8]/[10]: set_cookie at line 45 lacks secure/httponly/samesite; no compensating Django security settings exist.]

Auth cookie set without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags — The session token can be stolen via man-in-the-middle attacks on HTTP connections, via XSS, or used in CSRF attacks. Session hijacking leads to full account takeover. [verified: Same missing-cookie-flags finding as [2]/[5]/[8]: set_cookie at line 48 omits secure/httponly/samesite flags, verified against source and settings.]

auth_token cookie set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags — Session tokens can be stolen via XSS or network sniffing, and the application is more vulnerable to CSRF attacks, leading to full account takeover. [verified: response.set_cookie('auth_token', user.auth_token) at line 50 sets no httponly, secure, or samesite flags; settings.py contains no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE/CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY/SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, so the flags are genuinely absent.]

Unrestricted File Upload without content or extension validation — Attacker can upload arbitrary files including malicious scripts, and when combined with the path traversal in the filename, write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem. If backup=true, achieves OS command execution. [verified: Same upload sink as finding 1 with the additional note that backup='true' feeds the filename into os.system() for command injection; still no upload-content validation.]

IDOR — Message Forgery via Attacker-Controlled creator_id — Any authenticated user can send messages that appear to originate from any other user (including admins), enabling impersonation, social engineering, and trust-boundary bypass. [verified: Same vulnerability as finding 1: line 26 reads creator_id from untrusted POST body, line 27 uses it directly in User.objects.get(user_id=cid) with no ownership verification against the authenticated current_user, enabling message forgery by any authenticated attacker.]

IDOR — attacker-controlled creator_id allows message sender impersonation — Message forgery — attacker can send messages appearing to come from any user (CEO, admin, etc.) [verified: cid = int(request.POST['creator_id']) at line 27 is attacker-controlled form data with no server-side validation that cid equals current_user.user_id; @user_is_authenticated only validates the auth_token, so any authenticated user can impersonate any sender.]

IDOR — Unauthorized Read/Delete of Any User's Messages — Any authenticated user can read private messages between any other users or delete them, violating confidentiality and integrity of the messaging system. [verified: At line 50-51, message is fetched via Message.objects.get(pk=message_id) using the attacker-chosen message_id with no subsequent check that message.creator or message.receiver matches current_user; lines 54-59 then render or delete it, giving any authenticated user full read/delete access to all messages.]

IDOR — Unauthorized Access and Deletion of Any Message — Any authenticated user can read private communications between any two users or delete arbitrary messages by enumerating message IDs. [verified: Message.objects.get(pk=message_id) at line 51 retrieves the message solely by URL-supplied PK with no sender/recipient ownership check against current_user; @user_is_authenticated only ensures a valid session exists, allowing any authenticated user to view or delete any private message.]

IDOR: Unauthorized deletion of Pay records via pay_id — Any authenticated user can delete direct deposit records belonging to any other user, causing disruption to payroll processing and potential financial data loss. [verified: Same IDOR as finding 0: @user_is_authenticated at line 70 only gates on cookie presence, and the Pay model's ForeignKey to User is never checked against current_user in the DELETE path, so any logged-in user can delete any pay_id.]

IDOR — any authenticated user can delete another user's direct deposit (Pay) records — An attacker with any valid auth_token can delete all direct deposit entries for every user in the system, disrupting payroll. [verified: user_pay DELETE handler at line 72 calls Pay.objects.get(id=pay_id).delete() using URL-supplied pay_id with zero ownership check; the @user_is_authenticated decorator only verifies a valid auth_token exists but never scopes the operation to the authenticated user's records, and sister endpoints (decrypt_bank_acct_num line 48, user_pay_index line 58) do filter by user=curr_user confirming the omiss]

Insecure auth_token Cookie — Missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite Flags on Signup — Session hijacking via network sniffing or XSS — attacker obtains auth_token set at signup and impersonates the newly registered user or any user whose token is captured, gaining access to all PII, payroll, and admin functions available to that account. [verified: The signup handler at app/views/users/views.py:35 calls response.set_cookie('auth_token', auth.auth_token) with no secure, httponly, or samesite flags on a publicly reachable POST /users/ endpoint, enabling session token theft via MITM or XSS.]

IDOR / horizontal privilege escalation — user_work_info_index exposes any user's PII via URL parameter — Any authenticated employee can view the salary, SSN, date of birth, bonuses, and years worked of every other employee by simply changing the user_id in the URL. [verified: Same IDOR at views.py:12 — User.objects.get(id=user_id) uses URL param unchecked; the @user_is_authenticated decorator (decorators.py:10) only queries User.objects.get(auth_token=…) without comparing the found user to the URL user_id — no ownership enforcement.]

IDOR — work_info view returns any user's PII (SSN, DoB, income) without ownership check — Any authenticated user can access any other user's full PII — SSN, date of birth, income, bonuses, years worked. [verified: Same IDOR at views.py:12 — user_work_info_index returns SSN/DoB/income via URL-derived user_id; auth decorator (decorators.py:5–17) does not enforce that the cookie's owner equals the URL user_id, unlike pay/retirement/messages views which call utils.current_user(request).]

IDOR — Horizontal privilege escalation on all user-scoped endpoints (work_info, pay, retirement, performance, messages, account_settings) — Any authenticated user can access any other user's full PII, payroll details, performance reviews, retirement data, and messages [verified: Same IDOR as finding 0 at views.py:12 — User.objects.get(id=user_id) with URL param and no ownership check; the decorator only validates token existence (decorators.py:10) without verifying the token belongs to the requested user_id.]

Denial of Service — unbuffered file upload reads entire file into memory — Server memory exhaustion; application crash or unresponsiveness. [verified: Benefits.save_data reads the entire uploaded file via uploaded_file.read() into a ContentFile at line 30 with no application-level size limit; Django's FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE only governs the upload spool, not this in-memory read of arbitrarily large files, enabling memory exhaustion DoS.]

Stored Cross-Site Scripting via mark_safe on User First Name — An attacker who registers with a first name containing JavaScript (e.g., `<script>steal(document.cookie)</script>`) will have that script execute in the browser of every authenticated user, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, and complete account compromise across the application. [verified: safe_name() at line 155-156 returns mark_safe(self.first_name) which bypasses Django auto-escaping; first_name is user-controlled via signup (views.py line 27) and account update with zero sanitization. Rendered in nav_loggedin.html line 23 on every authenticated page. Self-XSS but chainable via CSRF/social engineering.]

Stored XSS via mark_safe() on user-controlled first_name in safe_name method — Attacker can register with a first_name containing HTML/JavaScript (e.g., <script>alert('XSS')</script>), and the malicious script executes in the browser of any user viewing a page that renders the nav_loggedin template (every authenticated page) [verified: mark_safe(self.first_name) at line 155-156 bypasses Django auto-escaping; first_name is attacker-controlled (views.py line 27) with no HTML sanitization, rendered in nav_loggedin.html on every authenticated page.]

Stored XSS via mark_safe() bypass on user-controlled first_name rendered site-wide in navigation — Stored XSS — cookie theft, session hijacking, credential phishing for all users viewing the nav bar [verified: Same XSS as finding 1: mark_safe() on user-controlled first_name at line 155-156 with no HTML sanitization, rendered in nav_loggedin.html on every authenticated page.]

Stored XSS via mark_safe on user-controlled first_name rendered in navigation bar — Session hijacking via cookie theft, credential phishing, defacement, JavaScript keylogging on every page the victim loads. [verified: Same stored XSS via mark_safe(self.first_name) at line 155-156; first_name accepts arbitrary input from signup/account update forms with no validation or escaping.]

Static IV reuse per user in AES-CBC encryption weakening PII protection — Weakened confidentiality of encrypted PII — pattern leakage enables cryptanalysis of SSNs and bank account numbers [verified: Encryption.get_iv() retrieves a per-user IV from KeyManagement that is generated once at seed time (seed.py line 349) and never rotated — there is no IV-update path anywhere in the codebase. In AES-CBC, reusing the same (key, IV) pair across multiple encryptions of different plaintexts (SSN, bank account) leaks block-level relationships and violates the unpredictability requirement, with no compen]

Session auth_token not invalidated after password change — stolen tokens remain valid forever — An attacker who obtains a user's auth_token retains permanent access even after the victim changes their password. There is no way to force-logout all sessions. [verified: The pre_save signal in app/signals.py only calls generate_token() when instance.pk is None (line 11), so auth_token is never regenerated on password change via reset_password (password_resets/views.py:93) or user_view (users/views.py:78). The user_is_authenticated decorator (app/decorators.py) trusts any valid auth_token without server-side invalidation, and logout only deletes the cookie client-s]

Account enumeration via forgot_password — different responses for existing vs. non-existing emails — An attacker can build a list of valid employee email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or password reset attacks. [verified: forgot_password at line 16 returns different responses for existing vs. non-existing emails, allowing unauthenticated enumeration of valid user accounts.]

User Enumeration via Forgot Password Functionality — An attacker can compile a list of valid user email addresses for targeted phishing, password guessing, or password reset token attacks. Combined with the weak MD5-based reset token, enumeration enables targeted account takeover. [verified: forgot_password at lines 19-27 returns distinct messages ('An email was sent…' vs 'We do not have the email…') depending on whether the email exists, allowing unauthenticated enumeration of registered users.]

Open Redirect via Unvalidated POST 'path' Parameter — Attacker can redirect authenticated users to arbitrary external URLs after login, enabling credential phishing, malware distribution, or social engineering attacks. [verified: Same open-redirect data flow as [0]/[3]/[6]: POST path at line 33→HttpResponseRedirect(path) at line 48 (earlier line refs) with no validation; redirect target is unconstrained.]

Account enumeration via distinct login error messages — Attacker enumerates valid email addresses to target phishing or credential stuffing attacks. [verified: Duplicate of [7]: lines 56 and 58-59 produce distinct 'Email incorrect!'/'Password incorrect!' messages, enabling email enumeration via differential responses.]
